newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission takes up arms over BA-American deal.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission takes up arms over BA-American deal.

text.p: Fresh from its successful battle with Boeing Co, the European Commission is turning to British Airways, seeking concessions before it will approve its alliance with AMR Corp's American Airlines.

The EU's antitrust watchdog is reported to have asked the two airlines to release 350 weekly landing and taking off slots at London's Heathrow Airport, the world's busiest -- nearly double the number suggested by Britain's Office of Fair Trading.
To make things even more difficult, the Commission -- or more exactly, its competition chief Karel Van Miert -- objects ferociously to the airlines getting paid for any of the slots ceded.
The Financial Times said on Monday that the Commission had told the British government and the companies that it was looking for the release of 350 slots at Heathrow.
The spokeswoman for European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock, who is probing the merger together with Van Miert, would say only that the Commission is currently "looking at possible remedies."

But an EU source said the report was more or less on target, stressing that the Commission's position at this stage was a "maximalist" one, designed to secure the best concessions to safeguard competition on the U.S.-British air route.

The Commission's competition services concluded earlier this year that together the two airlines would control about 60 percent of passenger transport between Britain and the United States. On 13 transatlantic routes, the deal would eliminate competition altogether, they said.

This view is largely echoed on the other side of the Atlantic. The U.S.'s General Accounting Office, the investigative arm of Congress, presented a plan in June under which six U.S. carriers would get 23 daily roundtrips to Heathrow -- a weekly total of 322 take-offs and landings.

The Commission has in the past linked its approval of air alliances that would otherwise create or strengthen a dominant position to the release of slots for other airlines wishing to start or increase a scheduled service if the slots could not be obtained from the airports.

The idea is not so much to reduce passenger capacity as to cut down the number of flights operated by the two airlines. That would allow other carriers to operate at congested airports such as Frankfurt, Milan, Paris-Orly and Heathrow, where the slots are to a large extent monopolised by the domestic airlines and other well-established carriers.

The Commission is unlikely to give its final decision on the BA-American alliance before the autumn, possibly in October. Meanwhile, BA and American will have the month of August to mull a response to the Commission's demands, which will then be submitted to an advisory committee of antitrust experts.
The Commission stops practically all work during its annual August break.
It started its investigation into the BA-American link-up -- as well as Lufthansa's alliance with United Airlines, Dutch airline KLM's with Northwest Airlines Corp and other linkups -- in July 1996.
Britain's Office of Fair Trading proposed last year to clear the BA alliance on the condition that the airlines give up 168 weekly slots at Heathrow.

The Commission will give its formal blessing on Wednesday to the planned $16 billion merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas after a long and bitter investigation which brought the E.U. and the U.S. close to a potentially damaging trade war.
